newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Russian 97 budget gap seen hard to cover.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Russian 97 budget gap seen hard to cover.

text.p: A commission set up to iron out Russia's 1997 budget draft on Friday agreed to widen the projected deficit and raise foreign borrowing but analysts said it was not immediately clear how the gap would be closed.

The conciliation commission of government and parlaiment, set up after the State Duma lower house rejected the first draft budget, agreed to widen the deficit to 3.5 percent of gross domestic product from a previous 3.3 percent.
"Instead of discussing the magnitude of the budget deficit, the members of parliament should think seriously about the sources of finance," said Pavel Teplukhin, chief economist at Troika-Dialog.
It was not immediately clear whether the wider gap would result from increased spending or lower revenues.
But first deputy finance minister Vladimir Petrov said the government would increase foreign borrowing by 4.00 trillion roubles ($732 million) as a result.
"Another $700 million without significant commitments from foreign governments? I don't see how it is going to be possible," Teplukhin said.
Russia's main source of foreign borrowing next year are likley to be some $4 billion of a three-year $10 billion International Monetary Fund and and Eurobond issues.
However, the IMF has effectively delayed payment of the latest tranche because of concern over the low level of tax collection and its possible impact on the budget deficit.
Partly as a result of a tough monetary policy which has slashed inflation to under two percent from 18 percent in January 1995, the economy is starved of cash and wages and taxes are going unpaid.
The government has been under intense pressure in drawing up the deficit, trying to keep within the terms of the IMF loan but also facing demands from deputies for more spending.
"Any weakening of the budget deficit is at first glance a cause for concern," said a Western economist in Moscow.
The economist added that increasing foreign borrowing would not at first glance be inflationary, but it could spark price rises if the borrowed funds were turned into roubles.
The conciliation commission agreed on Friday to base the budget on an annual inflation rate of 11.8 percent, the higher of two scenarios originally proposed.
The panel also agreed on a forecast for GDP of 2,727 trillion roubles, implying real growth of two percent.
It also assumed a weaker rouble exchange rate of 5,750 to the dollar, compared with 5,560 in the draft.
Arkady Dvorkovich of the finance ministry's foreign expert group said this could raise revenues by two trillion roubles, but would raise foreign debt service costs.

He also believed the government would not find it easy to raise an extra four trillion roubles in foreign borrowing but said a possible source of finance could be an untied credit of up to a maximum $1 billion from the World Bank, though this had not yet been discussed.
"It is an option but the government doesn't want it," he said. ($1=5463 Rouble)
